items.title: The ongoing efforts to get ecocide recognized at the International Criminal Court

s: Activists want to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment and punish those responsible for defiling it
An aerial view of the 2010 Deepwater Horizon oil spill in the Gulf of Mexico, the largest marine oil spill in history.
Under the proposed ICC amendment, oil company executives could be held accountable in such cases.
Image via Wikimedia Commons.
CC BY-SA 2.0.
In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law.
The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations.
Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “ digital nation ” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago.
In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment.
As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations.
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations.
Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook. Fair use.
It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis.

These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.
Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible.
This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.
Vanuatu was the first state to call for ecocide to be added to the ICC in 2019.
In announcing the proposal, Regenvanu said:
“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC.
Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”
A protest poster against ecocide shaming oil giants at a climate protest in Maryland in 2017.
Photo from Wikimedia Commons.
CC BY-SA 2.0.

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

items.title: Why Japan’s anti-hate measures fall short

s: Japan is yet to establish the Human Rights Protection Bill and a independent national human rights institution
Anti-immigration policy protest in Oct 2026.
Screen capture from the Japan Unfiltered YouTube Channel. Fair Use
A newborn Black baby delivered at a clinic in Tokyo’s Meguro Ward became the target of a barrage of racist harassment online.
The clinic published the baby’s photo with a congratulatory message on its social media account as part of its routine “babies born this month” photo series.
A screenshot of the post spread widely on X, gaining more than 1.3 million views within a day.
The post attracted many hateful comments loaded with anti-immigrant sentiment and racial discrimination against non-white and non-Japanese people.
Some of the hateful comments received thousands of likes.
All comments have since been removed from the post, and the clinic has disabled commenting on its Instagram.
This incident sheds light on two issues within Japanese society.
On one level, it reflects how racist hate speech still remains rampant in Japan.

But more broadly, it exposes a missing layer of justice infrastructure: Japan has no independent human rights commission empowered to handle discrimination complaints, no enforceable national hate speech law, and no effective way to force platforms to remove hate speech targeting entire groups.

While some cultural critics argue that the widespread racial discrimination in Japan stems from the younger generation’s inadequate interest in foreign cultures and development, others argue that the prevalence of online hate speech is to a large extent related to a lack of effective domestic legislation and human rights education.

Despite being a signatory to the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD) since 1995, Japan has not passed the Human Rights Protection Bill or established an independent national human rights institution to investigate human rights violations and penalize perpetrators.
While there have been numerous attempts to pass such a bill, it was tabled multiple times in the 2000s and early 2010s.
Critics say the efforts failed because the public feared it could violate the freedom of speech protected by the Constitution.

Thus, instead of passing a comprehensive set of laws, it addresses discrimination and human rights through issue-specific laws, such as the Act on the Promotion of Human Rights Education and Human Rights Awareness-Raising (2000), the Act for Eliminating Discrimination Against Persons with Disabilities (2013), the Act on the Promotion of Efforts to Eliminate Unfair Discriminatory Speech and Behavior against Persons with Countries of Origin other than Japan (2016), the Act on the Promotion of the Elimination of Buraku Discrimination (2016), as well as the Act on the Promotion of Public Understanding of the Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (2023), which aim to raise public awareness about human rights and providing government support rather than criminalizing hate speech and discrimination.

For example, while the Hate Speech Elimination Act was enacted to curb xenophobic street rallies that terrify ethnic minorities residing in Japan, such as the series of protests against Kyoto Korean Elementary School between December 2009 and March 2010, it does not declare hate speech illegal, nor penalize offenders with fines or jail sentences.
Moreover, the law only protects foreigners with a legal status, but excludes undocumented migrants, asylum seekers, and Indigenous peoples, including the Ainu and Ryūkyūans.

The law’s legal scope is at odds with the United Nations’ recommendations, which state that a signatory of the ICERD must “ensure legislative guarantees against racial discrimination apply to non-citizens regardless of their immigration status, and that the implementation of legislation does not have a discriminatory effect on non-citizens.

Legal experts have criticized the restrictive clause of the law for, as Shuji Oda, president of the Dai-Ichi Tokyo Bar Association, says, “giving rise to a false reverse implication that hate speech directed at individuals without legal residency status is permissible.”

items.title: In Moldova, teens are learning about democracy and elections through an app

s: The app gives short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Moldova is a relatively small post-Soviet state with a population of three million people.
A landlocked country, it has a long border with war-torn Ukraine and Romania; with the latter, it shares the same official language.
The territory that is now Moldova was once part of the Russian Empire, and later the Soviet Union, and Russia has been meddling in its affairs.
Moldova has a large Russian-speaking population and a problematic unrecognized territory: Transnistria, which is basically controlled by Russia.
It also has European aspirations and was officially named a candidate to join the European Union in 2022, after Russia invaded neighbouring Ukraine.

The country’s most recent parliamentary elections were held in September 2025, and despite the record influx of Russian disinformation and other meddling, elections were recognized as fair and democratic by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OCSE) observers.
The pro-European Party of Action and Solidarity (PAS) won the elections with a small majority.
The initiative supported by Digital Spark is an app called VotEDU, which answers basic questions about the democratic institution of elections for high school students in Moldova.

It does so through short, interactive lessons using quizzes, flashcards, and other easily accessible formats in three languages: Romanian, Russian, and English, and is the subject of this Spotlight story.
Global Voices interviewed the app’s developer, Vlad Garbuz, about the impact of Digital Spark and his initiative.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Vlad Garbuz (VG): I started VotEDU, an independent civic-education project in Moldova, to help young people understand democracy before they vote for the first time.
The idea began at the VOTech hackathon in Moldova.
I joined Digital Spark because I wanted to turn it into a tool that students could use in everyday life and teachers could bring into class.
The project helped me build the app and begin testing it with the young people it is meant for.
GV: What issue or challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
VG: Young people meet politics every day through their feeds, long before they enter a polling station.
In Moldova, many young people encounter misleading claims online.
Yet many have very few easy ways of asking questions about elections and getting the answers they can understand.
That made me wonder how civic education could reach young people in the spaces where they already spend their time.
VotEDU was the answer.
It puts short lessons, simple explanations, and activities on their phones, so they can learn at their own pace.
GV: What are the key changes or activities that you implemented during your participation in the project?
VG: During Digital Spark, VotEDU developed into a civic-education app with nine units, 28 short lessons, quizzes, interactive activities, and a glossary of 136 civic terms.
The content is available in Romanian, Russian, and English.
All of the lessons have been reviewed for accuracy and political neutrality.
Student privacy guided the app’s design.
A short guide was also prepared for teachers.
VotEDU was represented at Moldova Digital Summit 2026, where several educators expressed interest in trying it in schools.
The app is now being piloted with high school students in Moldova through its web version.
It is also available on the App Store, with the Google Play version coming soon.

items.title: Support Global Voices’ December Spotlight: Digital Communities

s: Donate to our Digital Communities Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!

Digital communications sparked new ways of forming communities: communities that spanned vast distances; that offered asynchronous interaction, innovative forms of constructing identities, and potentially enormous reach.

These communities have provided connection for people who are isolated or marginalized, built powerful groups around both professional interests and unusual hobbies, and facilitated astonishing feats of knowledge-sharing and organizing, from Wikipedia to academic sub-field networks to hobby groups and fandoms.
But digital communities bring new challenges as well, from questions of moderation to questions of ownership.
Almost all of them are built on the backbone of infrastructure owned by Big Tech — hardware at a minimum, usually several layers of software as well.
This is a risky place to put trust.

Witness the sudden devastation when a platform is bought and sold, and what was accessible and inclusive becomes hostile; or the sudden change-to-terms-of-service maneuver, when a company leverages the trust of its users to exploit them for their sellable data.
Increasingly hollowed-out echo chambers — toxic or just obliviously navel-gazing — make digital communities difficult and often dangerous to navigate.
The proliferation of targeted ads, the risks of rapidly spreading mis- and disinformation, and, more recently, the insertion of large language model bots all illustrate this.

Sometimes it feels like it’s impossible to resist the tidal wave of AI slop and bot content and the all-pervasive mistrust of information engendered by the sheer amount of misinformation and disinformation we have seen produced this decade.
But there are still ways to organize digitally.
The same social media that is polarizing Indian society is where young people have organized and continued to organize to resist the authoritarian Modi government.
In Brazil, supporters of President Lula ran an organic, human-driven campaign that successfully beat algorithms weighted toward his opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, in the October 2026 election.
LGBTQ+ people in hostile environments often only have online spaces to find community and solidarity.
People everywhere are rewilding the internet, reclaiming, reviving, and rebuilding communities everywhere in defiance of faceless, consolidated power.
In this month’s spotlight, Global Voices, in partnership with Ranking Digital Rights, will explore the multiverse of digital communities — starting with our own.

We want to highlight specific communities, the tools and tactics they use to organize, resist, and overcome the algorithmic pressure from tech platforms, and show how digital communities thrive and persist the world over, defying overwhelming power asymmetries and rejecting pressure to accept the defaults.

items.title: Family stories keep alive Georgia’s democratic past and the memory of Soviet repression

s: In the Guria region, an organization is helping people recover a history the Soviets tried to erase
Resort in the Guria region of Georgia.
Photo by Tinari.totoro on Wikimedia Commons ( CC BY-SA 4.0 ).

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Guria is a region in Georgia, situated in the southwestern part of the country.

It has a coastline on the Black Sea to the west, which is about 22 kilometers (13 miles) long, and the region is bordered by the Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region to the north, Imereti to the east, and the Autonomous Republic of Adjara to the south.
It has a rich history and a historical tradition of democracy.
Today, in the region, independent media access is limited and digital literacy remains low.
However, Guria has a civic tradition that most of its own residents do not know about in detail.

In 1904, locals organized protests against imperial (Russian, at the time) institutions, formed institutions of self-governance, and proclaimed the Gurian Republic, an early experiment in participatory democracy.

The republic was violently suppressed first by the Russian tsarist empire, and later all the memories of it were fragmented further by decades of deliberate erasure under Soviet occupation of Georgia (1921–1991) and by repressions.
This is exactly what the Digital Spark Spotlight project in Georgia focused on: history and memory in the Guria region.
Global Voices interviewed Lika Mergaladze, head of the organization Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, about their project: what they have done and what they learned through it.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about yo ur organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project?

Lika Mergaladze (LM): Our organization, Komli Initiative for Civic Engagement, works to preserve local history, strengthen civic engagement, and promote sustainable development in the Guria region of Georgia.
We use exhibitions, workshops, digital storytelling, and collaborative activities to connect communities with their history and encourage active participation in civic life.
We chose to get involved in the Digital Spark project because we saw an opportunity to combine local history with modern digital technologies.
We wanted to help community members document and share their family stories, develop digital skills, and better understand the connection between the past and present.
We believe that preserving historical memory and encouraging critical thinking are essential for building an informed and active community.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
LM: One of the main challenges in Guria is that many important historical stories have been forgotten or remain untold.
These stories were purposely erased during the Soviet Union.
Many families who were the victims of a series of repressions in the 1920s and 30s learned to remain silent about their past in the 50s after W orld War II.
As a result, younger generations often know very little about their ancestors and the region’s democratic traditions, including the Gurian Republic of 1904.
Another challenge is limited access to independent media and low levels of digital literacy in local communities.
The dominance of social media and television as information sources makes media literacy and critical thinking particularly important.

We undertook this project to address these challenges by helping local people preserve their history, recognize misinformation and propaganda, and use digital tools to share their stories with a wider audience.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

items.title: ‘Who will respond?’: Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong fears being forgotten amid 10-year sentence

s: The activist admits his mental state has been negatively affected by the 10-year sentence increase
Joshua Wong released from Lai Chi Kok Reception Centre on June 17, 2019.
HKFP's File photo.
In a letter from a Hong Kong prison earlier this year, jailed activist Joshua Wong expressed dread over the looming sentence in his foreign collusion case.
“Fretting about whether it’s 2032 or 2037, my mental state is hardly all right,” he wrote in Chinese, weighing when he might regain his freedom.
The agony inevitably stems from this: What if it’s 2037?
Well, it’s easy [for people] to sympathise in the moment, but it’s difficult to be consistent, and it will only get harder.

The 30-year-old pro-democracy activist has already spent almost six years behind bars over various offences and was set for release in January 2026, until authorities charged him last year with conspiring to collude with foreign forces — the second case against him under the Beijing-imposed national security law.
His case is one of the most high-profile examples of changing judicial norms in Hong Kong.
A prison letter Joshua Wong wrote to friend and former fellow student activist Louis Lee in February 2026.
This photo was taken on September 30, 2026.
Photo by Kyle Lam/HKFP.
Used with permission.
On November 5, just two months before he was due to be released, a court sentenced him to 10 more years in prison for colluding with foreign forces.
He is now expected to serve until late 2036, when he turns 40.
Standing in the courtroom as his new sentence was announced, Wong shook his head slightly and made notes, but appeared calm.
Judge William Tam ruled that Wong’s offence was one of a “grave nature” under the national security law, which carries a minimum penalty of 10 years in jail and up to life imprisonment.
The judge knocked off three years from a 13-year starting sentence for Wong’s guilty plea.

In prison correspondence shared with HKFP by two close friends ahead of Wong’s sentencing, the former poster child of Hong Kong’s democracy movement had at times reflected on the weight of facing an additional decade behind bars.
He expressed anxiety over fading from the memory of his friends — and from society at large.
In one letter, Wong wrote:
I have no idea how much more I will lose in the passing of time.
Responsibility is, in fact, response-ability.
But who will respond?
I can’t help but ponder and doubt.

Once a pro-democracy activist dedicated first and foremost to Hong Kong’s political future, Wong began campaigning as a charismatic, eloquent student leader who dared to stand up to the authorities — even to Beijing.

Hong Kong is an overseas territory of China, and has increasingly been pressured to conform to China’s political goals in recent years, despite agreements that Hong Kong would retain “ a high degree of autonomy ” when handed over to China in 1997.
A Netflix documentary about him is succinctly titled “Joshua: Teenager vs. Superpower.”
Yet, after years behind bars, Wong has changed.
The teenager who focused single-mindedly on Hong Kong’s democracy movement has become even more caring for those around him despite being separated by prison walls, according to his friends.
Tiffany Chin, a former student activist who campaigned alongside Wong, said.
The pair were once romantically involved and are now friends. She shared:
For me, it doesn’t feel like we’re the only ones supporting him.
In fact, he has been supporting people on the outside in his own way.
And, with the political causes he once championed now firmly crushed, Wong has turned inward to reflect on himself.
In another letter, he wrote:
We had held such high aspirations for society from a young age, we should hold ourselves to the same standard.
Only by refusing a life of mediocrity can we be worthy of the world we envisioned.

items.title: An AI chatbot can explain your rights. But can it get you justice?

s: Imagine a woman facing eviction who turns to an AI chatbot for help.
It explains her rights and drafts a letter to her landlord.
But she cannot afford a lawyer, does not know where to submit the letter and has no institution that can enforce her rights fairly.
The chatbot has made the law easier to understand, but has it brought her any closer to justice?
A September 2026 study by UK organization JUSTICE and the Administrative Fairness Lab found that one in six UK respondents who had experienced a legal dispute had used an AI chatbot.
Researchers examined 77 conversations involving questions about rights, legal correspondence, complaints and court proceedings.
Yet they could not establish whether these interactions helped resolve the disputes.
We know more about how people use AI for legal help than whether it changes their circumstances.
That distinction matters.
An estimated 1.5 billion people worldwide cannot obtain justice for their problems.
HiiL’s Justice Needs Surveys, covering more than 150,000 people across 20 countries, show that only around four in 10 achieve a fair resolution.
AI could help address this gap, but it is important to understand where its contribution begins and ends.
People facing legal problems may not know whether what happened to them is unlawful, where to seek help or how to navigate an unfamiliar process.
Legal advice is expensive, services can be difficult to reach, and institutions intimidating.
Purpose-built AI tools can explain rights clearly, organize information, prepare documents and identify relevant services.
Voice-based tools may also reach people with limited literacy or without smartphones or reliable internet.
Early pilots are yielding promising results.

In Australia, Hear Me Out, developed by the National Justice Project and the University of New South Wales, helps people identify the appropriate complaints body, understand the process and prepare supporting documents.
Its pilot assisted more than 400 complaints, helping people turn experiences of injustice into complaints that can be pursued.
In Nigeria, Citizens’ Gavel’s Podus AI helps people understand their legal rights, draft petitions and complaints, and identify the government agencies responsible for addressing them.
Since its launch in March 2024, the platform has onboarded more than 33,000 users.
These are meaningful developments.
But the number of tools and people assisted tells us only part of the story.
What happens after someone submits a complaint?
Understanding rights does not mean being able to exercise them.
A tenant may know an eviction is unlawful but have nowhere to turn; a small business owner may prepare a claim but lack the means to pursue it.
A person experiencing domestic abuse may face practical, financial or safety barriers to seeking protection.
Another challenge is getting the other party to participate.
In dispute resolution, this is known as the “ submission problem,” a concept developed by economists William Landes and Richard Posner.
A process works only if both parties are willing to negotiate, accept mediation, or submit to a third-party decision.
AI may help prepare a claim, but it cannot persuade a landlord to negotiate, compel an employer to pay wages, or make a business respond.
Even when parties reach an agreement, there is no guarantee it will be respected.
Without mechanisms to support compliance and enforce outcomes, an agreement on paper may have little practical effect.
There is also a growing challenge for the institutions receiving complaints.
AI may make it much easier for people to submit them, potentially increasing demand on already overstretched public services.
Recent UK reporting describes public bodies, councils and courts receiving a growing volume of AI-assisted submissions, some lengthy, repetitive and difficult to assess.
Dubbed “AI clog,” the issue is not that more people are complaining — lowering barriers to redress is positive.
The problem is that institutions may lack the capacity and resources to respond.

items.title: Diversifying funding was supposed to protect civil society: It did not

s: ‘…stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep’
Activists hold a candlelight vigil to commemorate those who lost their lives in post-election violence in Tanzania in Nairobi, Kenya, on November 20, 2025.
Image by Anadolu Lucas-Mukasa courtesy of FORUS.
“Every one of our grants is annual and project-tied.
We have no reserves and no core funding, which means that stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep.”
That is how one civil society organization in Algeria described its finances to us in a recent survey.

It is a sentence many donors would recognize from their own grant files, and it captures a reality familiar to many organizations: years of navigating short-term grants, restricted budgets and uncertain renewals, with little room to plan beyond the next funding cycle.
For years, civil society organizations have been encouraged to diversify their income, develop new partnerships and build financial and capacity resilience.
But the latest — and many would argue the chronic — funding crisis is exposing the systemic retreat in development funding.
Alternative sources are scarce, civic space is under pressure, and the political environment is becoming increasingly hostile.
Official development assistance fell by more than 23 percent in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded, and is projected to fall even more in 2026.
Twenty-six of the 34 members of the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee cut their aid, and the US aid freeze that flooded headlines turned out to be just one part of a wider retreat.

To understand what this means in practice, the European Union System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EU SEE) consortium partners — Hivos, Forus, Democracy Reporting International, European Partnership for Democracy, Transparency International and Civicus surveyed organizations in their networks between August and September, receiving 195 responses from over 68 countries.
The findings reveal the scale of the disruption: three-quarters of respondents say their funding is lower than at any point in the past decade.

A third say more than half of their budget has been affected since January 2025, and 86 percent report harder terms, such as grants not being renewed, being reduced or cancelled or even more complicated compliance terms.
“The results show a perfect storm for civil society.
Funding is disappearing at the very moment many organizations are facing greater political pressure.

What’s being lost is not just programs and jobs, but the independent voices to defend rights, give voice to vulnerable communities, and hold power to account,” explains David Kode, program director of EU SEE.
The hardest hit were mid-sized, locally rooted organizations, despite having the most diversified funding.
Among them, 90 percent reported funding cuts, 77 percent lost staff or reduced programs, two-thirds scaled back advocacy and community outreach, and 59 percent became less vocal publicly.
These are organizations connecting communities with services, donors and local governments.
Responses to question 11 in the survey: From January 2025 until today, what percentage of YOUR organization's budget has been impacted by donor budget cuts?
Budget impact differs across organizational profiles.
Screenshot from the survey. Fair use.
“We have had to sacrifice even our own salaries from other private sources to keep the NGO open and those who received a monthly salary are now working ad honorem,” said a respondent from Honduras.
In Indonesia, some organizations put staff on unpaid leave, while others could pay only half of their employees’ salaries.
Yet the damage is not only monetary: almost half of respondents report reduced capacity for advocacy and about 40 percent say they have become less vocal or reduced their reach.
A third of the respondents report having less control over their own priorities, and some have moved away from contested areas of work to keep their funding.

items.title: Street medicine vendors are dangerously filling Haiti’s healthcare gaps

s: The ongoing security situation has made the country’s healthcare crisis worse
Haiti is a country with very few health facilities and a dearth of healthcare workers to meet people’s needs.
Public hospitals lack basic medical equipment, demand far exceeds staff capacity, and administrative problems are rife.

Other health centres, usually run by non-profit organisations, help some of the most vulnerable people, while private hospitals are few and far between, given that most Haitians cannot afford to pay for treatment there.
Even the wealthy are often forced to go abroad for treatment when faced with critical health issues.

This already dire situation became worse when gangs from the Viv Ansanm criminal coalition began targeting both public and private health facilities, looting many of them, stealing equipment, and even setting fire to some of the properties.
Health centres located in gang-controlled areas are often forced to close temporarily because of fights that break out between rival gangs.
Enter the challenge of street medicine vendors, mobile drugstores, and sellers operating from kiosks.
Practically everywhere you go — on sidewalks and public markets, inside bus stations and more — you can find hucksters selling medicine out of buckets and bags, or from small stalls.
These vendors have no professional medical training; yet they often “prescribe” drugs that have nothing to do with their customers’ health concerns.
Sold in questionable conditions on the street, in heat and dust, these “medicines” pose a serious danger to consumers’ lives.
No Haitian government has fought effectively against this issue.
Because most people cannot afford private health centres, they self-medicate, taking these drugs without medical advice.
In many cases, the drugs are either expired, spoiled, fake, or do not work as promised.
While licensed drug stores are operating, they are small in number compared to the many unauthorised vendors that line the streets.

In a YouTube video on the channel Sedney the Reporter with host Sedney Saint-Fleur, Dr Wellington Derameau, a doctor, pharmacist, and researcher who completed several specialised university training programmes in the United States and France, spoke about the problems in Haiti’s pharmaceutical sector.

That public concern over low-quality medicine led him, in collaboration with the University of Colorado and the Faculty of Medicine at the State University of Haiti, to test the quality of pharmaceuticals circulating across Haiti, particularly in the capital, Port-au-Prince.
In 2020, they published the first scientific paper, showing the results of tests in which researchers sampled roughly 258 boxes of antibiotics across 28 open-air markets in Port-au-Prince:
Nou te jwenn 6 antimikwobyen (antibiyotik) sou 11 ki pa t gen okenn konfòmite spèktr.
Sa vle di, lòske nou fè des analiz poussées, nou wè ke medikaman sa yo nou te ranmase nan lari a yo pa gen anyen pou wè ak medikaman, pa gen prensip aktif.
We found that six out of 11 antibiotic types failed basic spectral compliance testing.
Advanced laboratory analysis revealed that these street-bought products contained no active ingredients whatsoever.
Selling drugs without active compounds in this informal market leaves patients without effective treatment and accelerates antimicrobial resistance.
Dr Derameau highlighted cases where patients bought “amoxicillin” expecting a functioning antibiotic, but received capsules filled with starch:
Mache paralèl la fragilize mache legal la, se premye konsta pa m pa rapò ak sa, epi li mete an evidans movèz kalite medikaman yo.
The parallel market undercuts the regulated sector, directly contributing to the spread of substandard medicine.
Official statistics from the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP) for the 2025–2026 fiscal year underline the scope of the problem.

Across the nation, only 101 pharmaceutical companies, 49 storage drugstores, 49 import agencies, and three local manufacturing labs hold valid licenses, while some geographic departments lack any legal pharmaceutical representation.
This vacuum, Dr Derameau emphasised, feeds a real threat to public health:

items.title: In win against impunity, Indonesian court orders the reform of Military Justice Law

s: The court ruled that soldiers who committed criminal offenses should be tried by civilian courts
Constitutional Court of Indonesia in Jakarta.
Photo by Christophe95. Wikipedia.
CC BY-SA 4.0
Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years.
The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.
The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.
The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law.
They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers.

They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official.
The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.
Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”
Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”
During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law.
The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H.
Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.

He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength.
Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”
Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards.
Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

items.title: Civil society questions decree that could block access to telecommunications networks in Mozambique

s: Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression
Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025.
Photo by Wilson Thole.
Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension.
The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

Activists and civil society actors argue that the decree could enable restrictions on access to the internet and digital platforms — tools that have become increasingly central to the circulation of information, the organization of protests, and civic participation.
The approved text allows the state to suspend telecommunications services for up to 48 hours without needing a court order, reports Deutsche Welle.

Also, according to civil society organizations, the decree grants broad powers to authorities to intervene in telecommunications networks on grounds of national security or the maintenance of public order.

By appealing to the Ombudsman, the organizations are requesting an analysis of whether the decree is compatible with the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique, as well as Mozambique’s international commitments regarding human rights and freedom of expression.
In March 2026, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Américo Muchanga, denied that the measure restricted rights.
He defended it as a way to protect society in critical moments, strengthening the state’s capacity to manage crises and protect critical telecommunications infrastructure.
In discussions with Global Voices, various experts presented different interpretations of its potential impacts.
One researcher, who asked not to be identified for security reasons, recalls that several democracies around the world have legal mechanisms allowing temporary restrictions on communications.

For the researcher, political contexts where social demonstrations are frequently interpreted as threats to stability can make the application of this type of legislation particularly sensitive. He notes:
O que foi feito neste decreto é tentativa de legalizar toda e qualquer ação que o governo possa ter em uma situação de protesto social.
Na França existe, no Brasil existe, nos Estados Unidos existem.

Em qualquer parte em que exista alguma democracia, que chamamos a dita democracia consolidada, existem dispositivos estatais, governamentais, que limitam o acesso às comunicações, quando se entende que eles violam o direito de outras pessoas ou imposições em causa do próprio Estado.
Não é o decreto o problema.
O problema é como pode ser aplicado.
O nosso problema é que não há tolerância.

Tudo aquilo que parece ser protesto é visto como tentativa de subversão, tentativa de colocar em causa a ordem. É um problema histórico de governança e questão central na interpretação também do próprio decreto.
What was done in this decree is an attempt to legalize any and all actions the government might take in a situation of social protest.
It exists in France, it exists in Brazil, and it exists in the United States.

Anywhere there is some form of democracy, what we call so-called consolidated democracies, there are state, governmental mechanisms that limit access to communications when it is understood that they violate the rights of other people or impose demands against the state itself.
The decree is not the problem.
The problem is how it can be applied.
Our problem is that there is no tolerance.
Everything that looks like a protest is seen as an attempt at subversion, an attempt to jeopardize order.
It is a historical problem of governance and a central issue in the interpretation of the decree itself.

items.title: Making injustice legal: How Israeli law legitimizes apartheid, genocide and impunity

s: Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing
Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine.
Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr ( CC BY 2.0).
Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law.
Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law.
The two face two different legal systems.

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.
For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

A May 2025 report by Adalah, the legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel, documents how Israel moved settlement governance in Area C under civilian authority while Palestinians remain under military rule.
Adalah calls the arrangement a system of apartheid and de facto annexation.
Inside Israel, the Knesset keeps adding to the structure.
Adalah’s Discriminatory Laws Database listed over 65 laws that discriminate against Palestinian citizens of Israel or residents of the occupied territory in 2017.

Its November 2025 report reviews more than 30 further laws passed between October 7, 2023 and July 27, 2025, which Adalah says rest on the principle of Jewish ethno-national supremacy that the 2018 Nation-State Law enshrined.
In March 2026, the Knesset passed a death penalty law with 62 votes.
Adalah and four other Israeli rights groups argue its wording excludes Israeli Jewish perpetrators of similar offenses, so that in practice it applies only to Palestinians.
They have petitioned the Supreme Court to annul it.
The Israeli group Yesh Din has tracked police investigations into settler violence against Palestinians since 2005.
Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent ended without an indictment, and only about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction.
Most closures cited an unidentified suspect or insufficient evidence, which Yesh Din attributes to police failures.
In roughly half of the nearly 30 mass settler attacks it documented between 2023 and late 2025, soldiers or police were present.
Soldiers face similar odds.
In March 2026, the military’s top lawyer dropped charges against five reservists accused of severe sexual and physical abuse against a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention camp.
Yesh Din said only two indictments existed over soldiers’ conduct in the Gaza war.
Courts have not interrupted the pattern.
In March 2025, Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously rejected a petition by five Israeli rights groups seeking unimpeded humanitarian aid into Gaza.
The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, joining findings by Amnesty International and B’Tselem.

In October 2026, the commission added that Israel committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and that military operations since January 2025 caused the largest displacement there since 1967.
In July 2024, the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel’s presence in the occupied territory is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible.

It also found that Israel’s legislation and measures breach Article 3 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid.
In September 2025, UN experts criticized the failure to act on the General Assembly resolution that followed the ruling.
Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024.
In December 2025, its Appeals Chamber rejected an Israeli challenge and left the warrants in force.

The reaction to the warrants, like that to the UN findings regarding apartheid, genocide and crimes against humanity perpetrated by Israel, has contributed to the failure of international law in delivering justice.

items.title: Madagascar aims to support biodiversity by protecting marine areas

s: In Madagascar, biodiversity goals are being tested by funding challenges and local realities
A booth at COP17 showcases Madagascar’s local communities and biodiversity.
Photo by Sary nalain'ny mpanoratra.
Used with permission.

At the 17th Conference of the Parties (COP17) on biological diversity, held October 19–30, 2026, in Yerevan, Armenia, Madagascar reaffirmed its commitment to protecting its remarkable biodiversity and showcased techniques local community members have implemented.
The country further outlined its plans and priorities for the future and promoted the initiatives it is committed to in order to protect both its terrestrial and marine ecosystems.

This conference was also a strategic opportunity to strengthen green partnerships, develop new collaborations, and to engage with national and international stakeholders involved in biodiversity conservation.

To mark the occasion, Global Voices interviewed Tojotsara Ratefason, Director of the Directorate of Protected Areas, Renewable Natural Resources, and Ecosystems (DAPRNRE), part of the Madagascan government’s Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (MEDD), at this conference.

The interview focused on Madagascar’s role in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 30×30 global target, conservation funding, and the vital role of local communities, women, and young people in the sustainable protection of Madagascar’s natural heritage.
Raveloaritiana Mamisoa (RM): Where does Madagascar stand on implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework?
Tojotsara Ratefason (TF): Madagascar est confiante dans sa capacité à contribuer à l’atteinte de l’objectif mondial 30×30, aussi bien pour les écosystèmes terrestres que marins.
Notre pays dispose déjà d’un système d’aires protégées qui constitue un socle essentiel pour préserver sa biodiversité exceptionnelle.
Selon les chiffres que nous présentons, ce réseau compte 155 aires protégées terrestres et marines.
Il s’agit d’un acquis important sur lequel nous pouvons nous appuyer pour poursuivre nos efforts de conservation.
Madagascar dispose d’un cadre national de référence pour orienter ses actions en faveur de la biodiversité: la Stratégie et le Plan d’Actions Nationaux pour la Biodiversité (SPANB).
Ce document définit les grandes orientations du pays en matière de conservation, d’utilisation durable et de valorisation de son patrimoine naturel exceptionnel.

Il s’inscrit dans le cadre de la Convention sur la diversité biologique, à laquelle Madagascar est partie, et constitue un instrument essentiel pour traduire les engagements internationaux en actions nationales.
Mais la protection de la biodiversité ne se résume pas au nombre d’aires protégées ni aux superficies concernées.
Notre objectif est avant tout de préserver les écosystèmes, les espèces et les habitats naturels qui font la singularité de Madagascar.
Notre patrimoine naturel est unique au monde et nous avons la responsabilité de le transmettre aux générations futures.
Cette ambition implique également de renforcer la collaboration avec les communautés locales ( vahoaka eny ifotony), qui vivent au contact direct de ces ressources naturelles.
Leur participation est indispensable, car la conservation ne peut pas reposer uniquement sur les décisions du gouvernement.
Elle doit être portée conjointement par les institutions publiques, les gestionnaires des aires protégées et les populations qui vivent dans les territoires concernés.
Nous devons donc trouver les moyens de travailler ensemble, dans une démarche de responsabilité partagée.
Les communautés locales doivent comprendre l’importance de la biodiversité, participer à sa protection et pouvoir constater les bénéfices qu’elles peuvent tirer de sa conservation.

C’est également dans cette perspective que le Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement Durable cherche à promouvoir les emplois verts et les opportunités économiques liés à la biodiversité unique de Madagascar.

Notre richesse naturelle ne doit pas seulement être considérée comme un patrimoine à protéger: elle peut aussi représenter une source de revenus et de développement pour les populations, à condition d’être valorisée de manière durable.
L’enjeu est de permettre aux communautés de mieux connaître la valeur de leurs ressources naturelles, d’en être fières et de comprendre qu’elles ont tout intérêt à les préserver.

Lorsque les populations constatent que la conservation contribue à améliorer leurs conditions de vie, elles peuvent devenir des partenaires encore plus engagés dans la protection de leur environnement.

items.title: Learning under trees in the era of AI: The paradox of education in Mozambique

s: AI could help bridge educational inequality in a country where thousands of students still learn outdoors

In many communities across Mozambique, formal education still takes place in the open air, under trees, in improvised yards, or inside fragile structures that barely offer protection from the sun and rain.

These so-called outdoor classrooms are not an innovative pedagogical choice, but more often than not, the expression of a structural deficiency: a lack of infrastructure, a shortage of materials, and an estimated deficit of around 12,000 teachers in 2025.
During the rainy season (roughly November to March in Mozambique), the situation becomes more challenging.

In several regions, the school calendar must be adjusted to respond to inclement weather, such as heavy rains that disrupt classes and hinder the continuity of teaching between November and March each year.
In this context, the question arises: What is the place of artificial intelligence (AI) in an educational system that, in many areas of the country, is still fighting for the basics?
In rural districts of provinces like Cabo Delgado, Nampula, and Zambézia, it is common to find classes of students studying under trees.

The Minister of Education, Samaria Tovela, has been evaluating schedule adjustments because, while classes are frequently interrupted during the rainy season, concentration becomes a constant challenge during periods of intense heat.

Without proper blackboards or textbooks, and often with a single teacher responsible for several classes, the learning process becomes irregular and deeply unequal when one million students learn to read and write on the ground.
This scenario highlights a central problem: Learning depends on minimum standards that are not yet guaranteed in Mozambique.
At the same time, one of the biggest obstacles to introducing technologies like AI in rural African contexts is the lack of connectivity.
In Mozambique, about 73 percent of the population lacks internet access, according to 2024 data from the Ministry of Transport and Communications.
Regional inequalities limit these initiatives, despite some progress recorded in recent years.
This limitation directly affects the potential of solutions such as distance learning or digital learning platforms.
Another critical challenge is the linguistic and cultural dimension.
In Africa, where more than 2,000 languages are spoken, only a fraction — around 49 — are represented on digital platforms like Google’s translation service.

Integrating Mozambique’s Indigenous languages, such as Emakhuwa, Xichangana, or Elomwe, into digital educational tools could significantly increase students’ comprehension and engagement, especially in the early years of schooling.
However, implementing these solutions raises practical questions in contexts where access to technology is still limited.

The overwhelming majority of the Mozambican population speaks a Bantu language most frequently at home (81.7 percent), and a portion cannot speak Portuguese at all (41.9 percent), though it is the sole official language of the country due to its colonial history.

Despite this, the media, official government communications, and healthcare institutions continue to privilege Portuguese to the detriment of Bantu languages — the languages of the masses — which, activists argue, constitutes a form of social exclusion.
Emerging initiatives, however, show that it is possible to bridge this gap with the aid of technology.
In Johannesburg, for instance, tech startups are developing AI solutions tailored to African languages.
Offline tools, pre-loaded content, and digital pedagogical assistants are some of the possible solutions to address the deficiencies and limitations of Mozambique’s education system.

While the government does not yet have specific policies to integrate AI tools in schools, advocates say the state could play a central role in integrating technology into the daily lives of students and teachers.

This also involves investing in teacher training; ensuring basic infrastructure; facilitating energy access; and strengthening partnerships with universities, startups, and international organizations.

items.title: Letter from a jailed Azerbaijani political prisoner reveals deadly consequences of silence

s: The Trump administration’s blind eye to severe human rights violations in Azerbaijan is deadly for political prisoners
Bahruz Samadov being brought to Sabail District Court in 2024.
Image by Voice of America, via Wikimedia Commons.
Public domain.
Bahruz Samadov is an Azerbaijani political scientist, peace activist, and PhD candidate at Charles University in Prague, or at least he was until the summer of 2024.
On August 21, 2024, the State Security Service detained Samadov while he was visiting his grandmother in Baku.
Global Voices reported on his arrest at the time, as part of a wider crackdown on critics before Azerbaijan hosted COP29 in November 2024.
Samadov was one of the few Azerbaijani voices to oppose the 2020 Karabakh war.
In his writing for OC Media, Eurasianet and other outlets, he argued for dialogue with Armenia and criticized the expulsion of ethnic Armenians from Karabakh.
Prosecutors charged him with high treason based on his WhatsApp exchanges with Armenian peace activists and on publicly available information.
Samadov denied the charges and called himself a “prisoner of peace.
His lawyer argued that the prosecution’s theory of “ indirect espionage ” was vague and had no basis in case law.
On June 23, 2025, after a closed-door trial, the Baku Grave Crimes Court sentenced him to 15 years in prison.
The Baku Court of Appeal upheld the verdict in September 2025, and the Supreme Court did the same in September 2026.

Amnesty International, which considers him arbitrarily imprisoned, reports that he has been held in solitary confinement and denied medical care, and that he has twice attempted suicide, most recently in his Supreme Court hearing.
Below, Global Voices publishes a letter Samadov wrote from prison and asked us to share.

The 2024 summer holidays ended in a nightmare: while visiting Baku, my home city, from my doctoral studies in Prague, I was detained by the notorious State Security Service of Azerbaijan and soon was charged with “high treason.”

Studying the ideological tenets of the hegemonic regime in my homeland, I directly connected its durability to the conflict between Azerbaijan and Armenia, revealing the narratives of “national unity” under the “savior strongman.”
During and after the outbreak of the 2020 War in Karabakh, I criticized the deployment of military means.
Between 2021–2024, I partook in various conferences and meetings across Europe, presenting my perspective and calling for a meaningful and inclusive policy of peace and co-existence.
The Azerbaijani regime, having years of the crackdown experience, is aggressively intolerant to any kinds of contestation, and especially targets the independent academic voices.
When the repressive machinery was re-launched in late 2023, the regime started the total crackdown on civil society, independent media, politicians, and academicians.
In private communications, more than five political prisoners connected it to the worsened relations with the Biden administration.
The latter was highly critical to the human rights violations in Azerbaijan.
Weeks before leaving the White House, Blinken invited human rights defender Rufat Safarov to Washington to receive the Human Rights Defender Award.
Several hours after visiting the US Embassy in Baku, Safarov was arrested and accused of hooliganism and fraud.
It was an open signal to the US that the leaving administration had no power to endorse the Azerbaijani critical voices.
The Azerbaijani government acted differently with the Trump administration.
The August 8, 2025 meeting and the peace agreement was the soon-disappeared sign of hope for us.

Even if the peace agreement did not include any references to human rights, the current administration’s plans for the long-term involvement in the region brought hopes for at least minimal reforms in Azerbaijan.

items.title: While Russia tries to manipulate information, local civil society is teaching Armenians media literacy

s: A group of journalists and activists created ‘Verify This,’ a platform where users can find reliable information

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South.
It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.
Armenia is a small, landlocked country that has, for years, relied on Russian support in its long-term conflict with the neighboring oil-rich and authoritarian country, Azerbaijan.
However, Armenia received a blow from Russia in 2022–2023, when it was not supported by Russian military forces during its conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

In September 2023, Azerbaijan launched a large-scale military offensive, expelled the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh, dissolved the government of the region, and incorporated the territory into Azerbaijan.

After this incident, when Russia did not support Armenia with its peacekeeping troops, likely because Vladimir Putin was already engaged in a full-scale invasion and war with Ukraine, Armenia visibly changed its attitude toward Russia.
Armenian Prime Minister ​Nikol Pashinyan started to work in earnest towards the goal of European Union ⁠membership for his South Caucasus country and increased diplomatic communication with the US.
He was re-elected on June 7, 2026.
The election took place amid reports of Russian interference.

Reuters, citing anonymous Western intelligence officials and documents, reported covert Russian efforts to undermine Pashinyan and support pro-Russian candidates, including through disinformation campaigns.
These elections showed how information warfare has expanded beyond social media.
It now included fake news websites, AI-generated videos and material presented as reporting by reputable international media outlets.
According to the US-based disinformation monitoring organization NewsGuard, a Russia-linked campaign circulated 31 fabricated stories about Pashinyan in just one week.
The stories accused him of election fraud and of trying to drag Armenia into a war with Russia.
Some of this material imitated international media outlets such as France 24 and Politico.
Other stories impersonated Armenian news outlets, including Armenpress and CivilNet.
With the proliferation of generative AI, disinformation and propaganda campaigns have become increasingly sophisticated.
Armenia’s experience shows how these campaigns operate in a country moving away from its longstanding reliance on Russia.
At the same time, Armenian journalists and civil society are working hard to build media literacy to counter disinformation campaigns.
This Digital Spark Spotlight interview is about one of these projects — “ Verify First,” a platform where users can find reliable information.

Global Voices interviewed Armin Asryan, a member of the group of journalists, editors, and activists behind the media literacy project “Verify First,” which tackles Russian information manipulation and propaganda.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project.
Armin Asryan (AA): We are a group of enthusiasts, operating through the ‘Socio Club’ — Social and Information NGO — and dedicated to driving positive change in Armenia’s information landscape.
We chose to get involved with the Digital Spark project because we were thrilled to see an opportunity to actively contribute to a healthier, more reliable information space on social networks.

In response to the growing challenges of online misinformation, we developed a targeted initiative to produce six educational video reels focused on practical fact-checking techniques and media literacy, designed to equip everyday social media users with the tools to spot and counter misleading content.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?
AA: The Armenian social media space is heavily impacted by disinformation, low-quality content, and online hostility.
Every day, social media feeds reveal content that not only disappoints users but also generates widespread panic and fear.

items.title: How medical neglect killed Alfredo Díaz in a Venezuelan cell

s: The state deprived a former governor of medical care despite clear warning signs
Illustration made with AI by Runrunes.
Used with permission.
Read our special coverage on Venezuela’s fight for democracy and the political crisis that has unfolded since the 2024 presidential elections, after the documented allegations of electoral fraud.

This is the first installment of a series by Luis Carlos Díaz covering cases of torture, neglect, and cruel treatment against political prisoners, based on the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission.
Originally published in Runrunes and translated by Caracas Chronicles.
To kick off this series, it is worth examining how the latest report by the UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) on Venezuela was constructed.

Based on 213 confidential interviews with 121 victims, relatives, and witnesses, as well as forensic data and judicial documents, the report matches the rigorous evidentiary threshold of “reasonable grounds to believe.”
Despite the Venezuelan state’s complete refusal to cooperate, the FFM’s technical findings expose a crucial reality.

Following the United States’ military intervention on January 3 and the capture of Nicolás Maduro, interim president Delcy Rodríguez announced cabinet reshuffles, released hundreds of prisoners, and oversaw a decline in long-term detentions.

However, the United Nations (UN) found that at least 18 high-ranking officials previously implicated in human rights violations and crimes against humanity remain in key positions of power or military command, including Diosdado Cabello, Gustavo González López, Alexander Granko Arteaga, and Vladimir Padrino López.
The core architecture of state repression remains fully intact, providing the structural context for the individual cases documented in this series.
Before delving into the case of Alfredo Díaz, I want to address a question that often lingers when we discuss the UN reports: What is all this work actually for?
What happens to a report like this once it is published?
The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission was not created on a whim, nor was it meant to issue a general diagnosis and stop there.

It was established by the Human Rights Council under Resolution 42/25 in 2019, with a specific mandate: to document the most serious crimes committed in the country to combat impunity, ensure accountability for those responsible, and secure justice for victims.
This carries practical consequences, even if they are not immediate.
The FFM is an investigative body, one of only seven active mechanisms of its kind worldwide.
That alone underscores how extraordinary our situation is, and how resilient civil society has been in organizing to secure its renewal on four separate occasions.
In October, countries in the Human Rights Council voted to extend its mandate for two additional years.

Whenever the FFM concludes there are “reasonable grounds to believe” that an individual participated in a human rights violation, that finding is preserved in secure databases with case files, testimonies, and evidence.
This material is not lost, even if no Venezuelan court is willing to use it.
This documentation has already had real effects outside Venezuela.
The report notes, for instance, that a federal court in Argentina issued an extradition request in June 2026 against a Spain-based former Venezuelan military officer linked to the 2014 repression.

The court relied on the principle of universal jurisdiction — the legal framework allowing a country to prosecute grave international crimes committed elsewhere, when justice is denied in the country of origin.
That officer was named in the 2025 special report on the Bolivarian National Guard.

items.title: Ecuadorian youth unite against neoliberal models and state violence

s: In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.
Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador.

Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center.
The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse.
Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse.
Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents.
Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old.
Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month.

The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million.

The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.
Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest.
Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

items.title: Trinbagonian Jason Jones wins landmark Privy Council judgement deeming ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional

s: Trinbagonian LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones at the Hall of Justice in Port of Spain, Trinidad, after the landmark 2018 judgement that deemed Trinidad and Tobago’s ‘buggery laws’ unconstitutional.
Photo by Maria Nunes, used with permission.

Eight years and nearly seven months after Justice Devindra Rampersad ruled, in the case of LGBTQ+ activist Jason Jones vs. the Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago, that Sections 13 and 16 of Trinidad and Tobago’s Sexual Offences Act Chapter 11:28 — which criminalise anal sex between consenting adults — were “unconstitutional,” the United Kingdom’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, still Trinidad and Tobago’s highest appellate court, overturned a 2025 Court of Appeal decision to keep the country’s “buggery law” on the books.
It has been a long road to get to this point.

Almost as soon as the 2018 judgement went in Jones’ favour, the Trinidad and Tobago government announced its intention to appeal, with then Attorney General Faris Al-Rawi stating, “The rights of equality in the Constitution are clearly expressed.
A first-instance decision is not the only decision to rely upon to settle the law. [An appeal] is only prudent so we can conclusively put the matter to rest.”
Almost seven years later, on March 25, 2025, a local appeal court overturned the 2018 judgement.
Jones was disappointed but not deterred, vowing to take the case all the way to the Privy Council.
He remained true to his word and on November 10, 2026 — quite ironically, given that it was a colonial-era law — British lawlords finally ruled on the matter.

There were a few key issues to be considered, including how to address the controversial “savings law” clause in the legislation — laws enacted prior to colonised countries becoming independent and developing their own constitutions, that were “saved” to remain in force even afterwards.

Jones maintained that the clause had “no place in a 21st century democracy” and that Trinidad and Tobago’s government and parliament were “derelict” in not removing it, especially after the twin-island nation became a republic in 1976.

The Council’s conclusion in the case, which deemed that “Sections 13 and 16 of the SOA 1986 have been shown by Mr Jones ‘not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual,’” caused it to agree with the 2018 ruling and deny the attorney-general’s cross-appeal.
With other regional territories also using the Privy Council as their highest court of appeal, the result could augur well for similar actions across the wider Caribbean.

As Jones told reporters on the steps of Trinidad’s Hall of Justice following his 2018 triumph, “The human rights issue is not just local […] Over 75 million Commonwealth citizens are criminalised using similar laws — 37 Commonwealth nations — criminalised similarly to Trinidad.”

Still, Jones — who launched his legal challenge in 2015 — says that the fight continues: “Whilst I welcome this judgement, it does not, however, address the main issues of human rights and equality for LGBTQ+ people which have been denied using British colonial-era laws across the Commonwealth and beyond.
It is a stance echoed by many LGBTQ+ organisations, as issues of discrimination, language, and societal and religious acceptance also persist.
Jones is well aware that changing these attitudes requires broader reform and re-education.
The law lords’ unanimous, provisional view, however, was that the original High Court remedy should stand.
However, there may well be written submissions still to come.

items.title: Can regenerative school gardens strengthen food security in Cameroon?

s: The school gardens are helping alleviate food insecurity while providing learning opportunities and empower community members
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre preparing the farm.
Photo by Support Humanity Cameroon.
Used with permission.
Students of Blessed Bilingual Education Centre in Ebang, Cameroon’s Centre Region, have recorded their first harvest of the 2026–2027 school year.

Through the Climate Change and Innovation Club, an initiative introduced in 2024 by Support Humanity Cameroon (SUHUCAM) to connect environmental education with practical action, students planted huckleberry in their school garden at the start of the academic year in September.

Like them, pupils in Cameroon’s North West Region are managing school gardens and growing food using regenerative practices such as minimal tillage, composting, organic manure and fruit-tree grafting.
Cameroon continues to face a decade-long humanitarian crisis, contributing to food insecurity in the Anglophone regions and Far North, while displacing thousands of families.
Earlier this year, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies reported worsening hunger among nearly 6,000 Cameroonian households following an assessment.
More than 3.3 million people were struggling to find enough food, while about 64 percent of households experienced severe food insecurity.
Children are among those affected.
Nationwide, 29 percent of children under five experience chronic malnutrition.
